Scope here is [bench/verification_chain.py](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/verification_chain.py); the Experiment 15 scheduler items sit outside this artifact, so this pass reports persistence-layer misses I could verify directly.

FINDING_ID: VC_F001
SEVERITY: 0.78
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.62
DESCRIPTION: `verify_record()` is not a safe chain-validity check. It directly calls `_verify_single()` for the requested index, and `_verify_single()` trusts the stored `chain_hash` of the previous record instead of first verifying that predecessor. I verified that corrupting record 0 in place makes `verify_chain()` fail while `verify_record(1)` still returns `(True, "OK")`. A caller can therefore get a false positive on record `n` even when the chain prefix is already broken.
PROPOSED_FIX: Make `verify_record()` verify the full prefix `0..index` before returning success, or rename it to something like `verify_record_self_consistency()` and document that it does not establish prefix integrity.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F002
SEVERITY: 0.74
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58
DESCRIPTION: Verification does not enforce the module’s own persisted-record schema. `_verify_single()` only special-cases `storage_mode == "full_payload"` and otherwise skips payload semantics entirely. I verified two tampered records that still pass `verify_chain()`: changing a stored record’s `storage_mode` to `"banana"` and recomputing hashes, and adding a forged `payload` field to a `hash_only` record and recomputing hashes. The result is that hash-consistent but semantically invalid records are accepted as valid.
PROPOSED_FIX: Add explicit schema validation during load/verify: allow only `full_payload` and `hash_only`; require `payload` for `full_payload`; forbid `payload` for `hash_only`; validate signature/attribution enums and required fields before treating a record as valid.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F003
SEVERITY: 0.63
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.39
DESCRIPTION: `append_record()` stores caller-owned `payload` and `metadata` objects by reference inside `sealed_body`. I verified that mutating the original Python dict after append changes the already-sealed record and causes later `verify_chain()` failure. This is an integrity foot-gun: an honest caller can corrupt the chain without touching the chain object again.
PROPOSED_FIX: Deep-copy or freeze `payload` and `metadata` before hashing/storing them, and return deep copies from mutating APIs so later caller mutations cannot rewrite sealed state.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F004
SEVERITY: 0.72
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.66
DESCRIPTION: Epoch verification has major blind spots. `verify_chain()` returns early when `self._records` is empty, so a file with zero records and arbitrary epochs is reported as valid. Even when records exist, `_verify_epoch()` only rejects `record_count > len(self._records)` and then hashes `self._records[:record_count]`; I verified that a tampered epoch with `record_count = -1` and the Merkle root of “all but the last record” still passes. Duplicate or reordered `epoch_index` values and arbitrary `sealed_at` values also pass because they are never checked.
PROPOSED_FIX: Always verify epochs, even on an empty chain; require `record_count` to be an integer in `[0, len(records)]`; reject negative slicing behavior; enforce `epoch_index == list position`, monotone `record_count`, and validate `sealed_at` if it is intended to be integrity-bearing metadata.
VERIFIED: TRUE
